analysis.one_liner: Lets Treasury clarify when workers must be treated as employees, not independent contractors, for payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 7 cosponsors, never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1978, a federal rule has blocked the Treasury Department from issuing guidance on whether workers should be classified as employees or independent contractors for payroll taxes. This bill would lift that ban, direct Treasury to write clear rules, and give businesses a buffer: no retroactive tax bills for past misclassifications unless the business had no reasonable basis for its treatment. It would also require companies that regularly hire contractors to tell them in writing which tax obligations they owe and which workplace protections they do not get, and it would strip reduced penalties from businesses that ignore the new guidance without a reasonable basis. The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are actually employees but are treated as independent contractors. Misclassification means they pay both the employer and employee halves of payroll taxes, and can be shut out of unemployment benefits, workplace safety protections, and employer-based retirement plans. The bill also benefits businesses that follow the rules and classify workers as employees, because misclassifying competitors undercut them on payroll tax costs. The Treasury and IRS also gain: misclassification is a major part of the federal tax gap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lifts the 1978 ban that stops Treasury from issuing any regulations or rulings on workers' employment tax status, allowing clear, uniform rules instead of decades-old uncertainty.

It requires businesses that regularly hire independent contractors to give them written notice of their federal tax obligations, the labor and employment law protections that do not apply to them, and their right to ask the IRS for an official status determination.
It ends reduced penalties for employers who lack a reasonable basis for treating workers as contractors, making deliberate misclassification more costly.

It protects businesses that acted in good faith: no retroactive payroll tax assessments for periods before a reclassification date unless the business had no reasonable basis for its treatment, and it preserves safe harbors for reliance on past audits, industry practice, or IRS rulings.

The bill's own findings state that misclassification contributes to the federal tax gap and can deny workers unemployment benefits, health and safety protections, and retirement benefits available to employees.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses whose business model depends on treating employees as independent contractors: they would face payroll tax liability, larger penalties, and the cost of reclassifying workers. Gig platforms, staffing firms, and others that rely on contractor classification would bear the biggest cost. Some workers who genuinely prefer contractor status would face a higher risk of being reclassified as employees.

drawbacks.text: Some workers genuinely prefer independent contractor status for flexibility and higher take-home pay, and clear guidance could push them into employee classification with withholding, schedules, and loss of independence they did not want.

Repealing the 1978 safe harbor (Section 530) entirely after a one-year transition removes a protection many small businesses have relied on for nearly four decades, and even with transition relief, reclassification raises labor costs for firms at the margin.

The bill preserves carve-outs treating certain professionals (including insurance salespeople and securities brokers) as non-employees for tax purposes, which weakens uniform treatment and preserves the status quo for those sectors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: workers who are employees in fact but treated as contractors lose unemployment insurance, safety protections, and retirement benefits, and the government loses payroll tax revenue, while businesses that play by the rules are undercut. The bill is deliberately designed to soften the cost to compliant businesses — no retroactive tax bills, reliance safe harbors, a one-year transition — which makes the design more balanced than a pure crackdown. The strongest honest objection is that contractor status has genuine value for some workers, and the bill's approach could reduce it; the bill answers that with notice requirements and the right to seek an IRS determination rather than blanket reclassification. On the whole, the benefits to misclassified workers and the level playing field outweigh the transition costs, which the bill substantially limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee never held a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Sherrod Brown on November 5, 2015, with five Democratic colleagues and one independent, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day.
No further action of any kind appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote in either chamber during the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017.

The bill was a reprise of earlier Fair Playing Field proposals; its purpose was to let Treasury finally issue worker-classification guidance that a 1978 law has prohibited for decades, while protecting good-faith businesses from retroactive tax bills.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses whose labor model depends on classifying employees as independent contractors kept the status quo: no new guidance, no tougher penalties, no notices to contractors, and continued payroll tax savings. Workers treated as contractors continued to pay self-employment taxes and forgo employee protections.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction (Sanders listed with the Democratic sponsors as an independent).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

against.name: Businesses reliant on independent-contractor classification
against.role: Gig platforms, staffing firms, and other contractor-heavy employers
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the existing ban on classification guidance; the bill would have raised their payroll tax and penalty exposure, giving them a strong stake in its failure.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Democrats or independents, no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the Republican-led Finance Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and staffing firms built on contractor labor
industries.note: The bill would let Treasury clarify when workers must be treated as employees, exposing these firms to payroll taxes, larger penalties, and reclassification costs. Their savings come directly out of workers' benefits and public tax revenue.

industries.industry: Financial services and insurance (brokers, agents, consultants)
industries.note: The bill preserves carve-outs keeping insurance salespeople, securities brokers, and other professionals outside employee status for payroll taxes, locking in contractor treatment for these sectors even as it tightens rules elsewhere.

industries.industry: Employers who classify workers as employees
industries.note: Clear national rules and tougher penalties on bad-faith misclassification remove the cost advantage of competitors who treat employees as contractors.

They gain clear prospective rules and protection from retroactive tax bills if they relied in good faith on audits, industry practice, or rulings, but the repeal of the Section 530 safe harbor after a one-year transition removes a protection they have held since 1978.
